questions.title: Usable hosts in a subnet
questions.prompt: A teammate gives you the subnet 10.0.5.0/28 and asks how many devices can actually be assigned an address on it. Walk through how you'd figure that out, and give the final number.
questions.modelAnswer: A /28 means 28 network bits out of the 32 total, leaving 32 - 28 = 4 host bits. The total address count in the subnet is 2^4 = 16 addresses. But not all of those are assignable to devices: the first address in any subnet is reserved as the network address (identifies the subnet itself) and the last address is reserved as the broadcast address (reaches every device on the subnet at once). So the usable host count is 2^(host bits) - 2 = 16 - 2 = 14 usable addresses. For 10.0.5.0/28 specifically: 10.0.5.0 is the network address, 10.0.5.1 through 10.0.5.14 are usable host addresses, and 10.0.5.15 is the broadcast address.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always work this the same way out loud, because it's easy to get the off-by-one wrong under pressure. Start with the mask bits: /28 means 28 ones, so 32 minus 28 leaves 4 bits for hosts. Two to the fourth is 16 total addresses in that block. Then I subtract exactly two, not because of some rule to memorize, but because every subnet reserves its first address to name the network and its last address for broadcast — neither of those can ever be handed to a device. So 16 minus 2 is 14 usable hosts. If someone asked me to size a subnet for, say, 20 devices, I'd immediately know a /28 doesn't fit and I'd need at least a /27, which gives 30 usable.
questions.example:
/28 = 255.255.255.240
Host bits = 32 - 28 = 4
Total addresses = 2^4 = 16
Usable hosts = 16 - 2 = 14

10.0.5.0/28:
  Network address:   10.0.5.0   (reserved)
  First usable host:  10.0.5.1
  Last usable host:   10.0.5.14
  Broadcast address:  10.0.5.15  (reserved)
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract 2 for the network and broadcast addresses
Confusing host bits with network bits (using 28 instead of 32-28=4 in the exponent)
Assuming the broadcast address is always .255 instead of calculating it from the actual mask
Not recognizing that the formula changes for a /31 or /32, which are special cases outside normal subnetting
keyPoints: Host bits = 32 minus the CIDR prefix length
Total addresses = 2 raised to the host-bit count
Usable hosts = total addresses minus 2 (network + broadcast)
10.0.5.0/28 has exactly 14 usable host addresses

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly derives host bits from the /28 prefix
Correctly calculates total addresses as 2^4
Correctly subtracts 2 for network/broadcast and states 14
Can identify the actual network, first/last usable, and broadcast addresses

questions.title: Containers vs. virtual machines
questions.prompt: Explain the real architectural difference between a container and a virtual machine — not just 'containers are lighter,' but what each one is actually virtualizing.
questions.modelAnswer: A virtual machine virtualizes hardware: a hypervisor sits between the physical host and each VM, and every VM gets its own full guest operating system kernel, believing it has its own CPU, memory, and devices. That's why a VM can run a completely different OS than its host and why VMs are measured in gigabytes and boot in tens of seconds to minutes. A container virtualizes the operating system instead: all containers on a host share the same underlying kernel, and isolation comes from kernel features (namespaces for what a process can see, cgroups for how much CPU/memory it can use) rather than a separate kernel per workload. That's why a container image is typically megabytes, starts in under a second, and why a Linux container can't run a Windows binary — it's borrowing the host kernel, not bringing its own.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I explain this in an interview is to point at exactly what's being virtualized, because 'containers are lighter' is true but doesn't show you understand why. With a VM, the hypervisor virtualizes the hardware, so every VM carries its own full kernel — that's genuinely heavy, but it also means strong isolation: a VM has no way to see another VM's kernel at all. With a container, there's no second kernel; every container on that host is a process (or group of processes) isolated by Linux namespaces and cgroups, but all of them are ultimately system calls into the one host kernel. That's the whole reason containers start in milliseconds and VMs take real boot time — a container isn't booting an OS, it's just starting a process inside walls the kernel already knows how to build.
commonMistakes: Saying containers are 'lightweight VMs' instead of explaining the actual kernel-sharing difference
Claiming containers are inherently less secure without acknowledging it's an isolation-model tradeoff, not an absolute
Forgetting that a Linux container can't run on a Windows kernel without a VM underneath it (as Docker Desktop does)
Not mentioning namespaces and cgroups as the actual kernel mechanisms providing container isolation
keyPoints: A VM virtualizes hardware via a hypervisor; every VM has its own kernel
A container virtualizes the OS; all containers share the host kernel
Isolation in containers comes from namespaces (visibility) and cgroups (resource limits)
This is why containers are smaller and start faster, and why they can't cross kernel types

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies what a VM virtualizes (hardware, via hypervisor)
Correctly identifies what a container virtualizes (the OS, shared kernel)
Names namespaces/cgroups as the actual isolation mechanism
Connects the architecture to the practical consequences (size, startup time, OS compatibility)

questions.title: The shared responsibility model across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
questions.prompt: Explain the cloud shared responsibility model, and how the line between 'the provider's job' and 'your job' moves depending on whether you're using IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.
questions.modelAnswer: The shared responsibility model says the cloud provider and the customer each own different parts of security and operations, and exactly where that line falls depends on the service model. The provider always owns the physical layer — data centers, physical hardware, the network backbone, and the hypervisor itself — in every model. In IaaS (like an EC2 instance or an Azure VM), the customer owns everything above the hypervisor: the guest OS, patching, the runtime, the application, and the data. In PaaS (like Azure App Service or AWS Elastic Beanstalk), the provider also takes over the OS and runtime patching, so the customer's responsibility shrinks to the application code, its configuration, and the data. In SaaS (like Microsoft 365), the provider runs essentially everything except how the customer configures access and classifies their own data. The customer is never fully off the hook, even in SaaS — identity, access configuration, and data classification stay the customer's job at every tier.
questions.professionalAnswer: I like to draw this as a sliding line rather than a fixed split, because that's what actually trips people up in interviews. At the IaaS end, I'm basically renting a VM, so I own the guest OS up — patching, runtime, app, data, all of it, same as if that box were sitting in my own data center. Move to PaaS and the provider has absorbed the OS and runtime patching for me, so my job narrows down to my code, my app-level configuration, and my data. By the time I'm at SaaS, the provider is running nearly the whole stack, and what's left on my side is really just identity and access — who in my org can touch what — plus classifying and protecting the data I put into it. The one thing that never moves, at any tier, is that the customer is always responsible for their own identity and access configuration and their own data. People who forget that are the ones who get surprised when a misconfigured S3 bucket or an over-permissioned SaaS app leaks data and assume that's 'the provider's problem.'
commonMistakes: Assuming the cloud provider is responsible for data breaches caused by the customer's own misconfiguration
Thinking SaaS means the customer has zero security responsibility at all
Not knowing which specific layers shift from customer to provider between IaaS and PaaS
Forgetting that identity/access configuration and data classification remain the customer's job in every single model
keyPoints: Provider always owns physical infrastructure and the hypervisor
IaaS: customer owns OS up through application and data
PaaS: provider also owns OS/runtime; customer owns app code, config, and data
SaaS: provider runs nearly everything; customer still owns identity/access and data classification

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states what the provider always owns regardless of model
Correctly describes the IaaS split
Correctly describes the PaaS and SaaS splits
Notes that identity/access and data classification remain customer-owned at every tier

questions.title: The Azure RBAC role-assignment equation
questions.prompt: A new hire asks you why they can view resources in the finance resource group but can't make any changes, while their teammate can both view and edit. Explain the Azure RBAC model that produces that difference, including the exact three-part equation behind every permission.
questions.modelAnswer: Every permission in Azure comes down to one equation: role assignment = security principal + role definition + scope. The security principal is the 'who' — a user, group, service principal, or managed identity. The role definition is the 'what' — a bundle of allowed actions, like Reader (view only) or Contributor (view, create, modify, delete, but cannot grant access to others). Scope is the 'where' — management group, subscription, resource group, or an individual resource, with permissions inheriting downward from broader scopes. The new hire's situation is almost certainly that they were assigned the Reader role at the finance resource group's scope, while their teammate was assigned Contributor at that same scope — same security-principal pattern, same scope, different role definition, and that one difference in role definition is the entire explanation for why one of them can edit and the other can only look.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk the new hire through the equation itself rather than just answering the specific question, because once they have the mental model they can self-diagnose this every time it comes up again. I'd say: every single permission in Azure is three things nailed together — who (the security principal), what they can do (the role definition), and where it applies (the scope). In this case, the 'who' and the 'where' are the same for both of you — you're both scoped to the finance resource group. The only variable left is the role definition: you've got Reader, which is read-only by design, and your teammate has Contributor, which includes create/modify/delete. I'd also flag the follow-up question they're likely to ask next — 'can I just make myself Contributor?' — and explain that's a conversation for whoever owns that resource group, since Contributor is a meaningfully bigger grant than Reader and shouldn't be self-service.
commonMistakes: Explaining RBAC only in terms of roles, without mentioning scope as an equally important variable
Confusing Contributor with Owner — Contributor cannot grant access to other people, only Owner can
Assuming a role assigned at the subscription level only affects that subscription's 'root,' forgetting it inherits down to every resource group and resource
Not recognizing that the security principal can be a group, not just an individual user, which is usually the better practice
keyPoints: Role assignment = security principal + role definition + scope
Reader allows viewing only; Contributor allows managing resources but not granting access
Scope can be management group, subscription, resource group, or resource, and inherits downward
Two people differing only in role definition, with the same principal type and scope, explains differing access

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the three-part role assignment equation correctly
Correctly distinguishes Reader from Contributor
Correctly explains scope and inheritance
Applies the model to explain the specific scenario in the prompt

questions.title: LRS vs. ZRS vs. GRS
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between Azure's LRS, ZRS, and GRS storage redundancy options — what each one actually protects against, and the cost/durability tradeoff between them.
questions.modelAnswer: All three keep three copies of your data, but differ in where those copies physically live. LRS (Locally Redundant Storage) keeps all three copies synchronously within a single datacenter — cheapest option, protects against drive or rack failure, but a full datacenter outage takes your data with it. ZRS (Zone-Redundant Storage) spreads the three copies synchronously across separate Availability Zones within the same region, so a single datacenter failure no longer takes down the data, at a modest cost increase over LRS. GRS (Geo-Redundant Storage) takes an LRS copy in the primary region and asynchronously replicates a second LRS copy to Azure's paired region, hundreds of miles away, protecting against a full regional disaster — something ZRS can't survive since it never leaves the region. The tradeoffs scale with the protection: GRS costs more because you're paying for storage in two regions, and because replication is asynchronous, a handful of the most recent writes could theoretically be lost in a true regional failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about this as three concentric circles of blast radius, and I always name what each one survives rather than just reciting acronyms. LRS survives a disk or rack dying — that's it, three copies, one building. ZRS survives losing that entire building, because it spreads the same three copies across separate Availability Zones in the region — same cost tier roughly, slightly more, for meaningfully more protection. GRS is the one that survives losing the whole region, because it's asynchronously shipping a second full copy hundreds of miles away to the paired region. The thing I always flag in an interview is that 'asynchronous' word — GRS isn't instant, so in a true regional disaster there's a small window of the most recent writes that might not have made it to the secondary yet. That's the real cost of GRS beyond the dollar figure: you're trading a small amount of potential data loss for regional disaster protection, and if you need to read that secondary copy even while primary is healthy, you'd reach for RA-GRS specifically.
commonMistakes: Thinking ZRS protects against a regional disaster (it doesn't — it never leaves the region)
Assuming GRS replication is synchronous, missing the real-world RPO gap it introduces
Not knowing all three options keep the same number of copies (three) and differ only in placement
Confusing GRS with RA-GRS — RA-GRS adds read access to the secondary; GRS alone does not
keyPoints: LRS: 3 copies, one datacenter — survives drive/rack failure only
ZRS: 3 copies spread across Availability Zones — survives a datacenter failure
GRS: LRS copy asynchronously replicated to a paired region — survives a regional disaster
Protection increases with cost, and GRS's async replication creates a small potential data-loss window

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what LRS protects against
Correctly explains what ZRS protects against
Correctly explains what GRS protects against, including the async tradeoff
Articulates the general cost-vs-durability tradeoff across the three

questions.title: Why IAM roles beat long-lived access keys
questions.prompt: Explain why AWS IAM roles are generally preferred over long-lived IAM user access keys for granting an application or service permissions.
questions.modelAnswer: An IAM user's access key pair is a long-lived credential: it doesn't expire on its own, it has to be stored somewhere the application can read it (a config file, an environment variable, a secrets manager), and if it leaks, it remains valid and exploitable until someone notices and manually rotates it. An IAM role, by contrast, is assumed temporarily — a service like an EC2 instance, a Lambda function, or another AWS account assumes the role and receives short-lived, automatically rotating credentials from AWS's Security Token Service, typically valid for an hour or so. There's no static secret to store or leak in the first place, because the credentials are generated on demand and expire quickly even if captured. That's the core security upgrade: roles eliminate the long-lived secret entirely rather than just managing it more carefully.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd frame this in an interview is that a long-lived access key is a secret you now have to protect forever, and a role is a secret you basically don't have at all. With an access key, I've created a credential that doesn't expire, so now I'm responsible for where it's stored, who can read it, rotating it periodically, and hoping nobody accidentally commits it to a repo — and if it does leak, it's valid until I catch it and rotate it myself. With a role, there's no persistent key sitting anywhere; whatever's running — an EC2 instance, a Lambda, another account — assumes the role and gets temporary credentials from STS that expire on their own, usually within an hour. Even in the worst case where those temporary credentials are captured, the blast radius is bounded by the expiry window, not by how fast I notice. That's why the real-world guidance is: use roles for anything AWS-to-AWS, and reserve IAM user access keys for the narrow cases — like a third-party tool that genuinely can't assume a role — where you have no other option, and rotate those aggressively.
commonMistakes: Saying roles are 'more secure' without explaining the actual mechanism (temporary credentials via STS)
Not knowing that role credentials auto-expire and auto-rotate, typically within about an hour
Assuming IAM user access keys are never appropriate, rather than acknowledging the narrow legitimate cases
Confusing an IAM role with an IAM group — a role is assumed for temporary access, a group is a way to attach policies to multiple users
keyPoints: Access keys are long-lived and must be stored, protected, and manually rotated
Roles are assumed and produce short-lived, auto-rotating credentials via STS
A leaked role credential has a bounded blast radius because it expires quickly on its own
Best practice: roles for AWS-to-AWS access, access keys reserved for narrow cases with aggressive rotation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why access keys are risky (long-lived, must be stored)
Correctly explains the role mechanism (assumed, temporary credentials via STS)
Articulates the practical security benefit of expiry
Gives a reasonable real-world guideline for when each is appropriate

questions.title: What a NAT Gateway actually does
questions.prompt: A private subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT Gateway instead of an Internet Gateway. Explain exactly what that buys you, and why an instance in that subnet can download a patch from the internet but nothing on the internet can open a connection into it.
questions.modelAnswer: A NAT Gateway gives instances in a private subnet outbound-only internet access: it lets them initiate connections out to the internet, but it never accepts an unsolicited inbound connection from the internet side. The asymmetry is exactly the point — the private instance can start a connection to download a patch, and the NAT Gateway forwards the response traffic back because that traffic is a reply to something the instance itself initiated. But nothing on the internet can start a new connection to the instance through the NAT Gateway, because the NAT Gateway has no mechanism to route an unsolicited inbound request to any specific private instance — it only ever tracks and returns traffic matching an outbound flow it already saw. A NAT Gateway is AWS-managed, needs an Elastic IP, and must itself live in a public subnet, not the private subnet it serves.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the asymmetry concretely rather than just saying 'outbound only,' because that's the part people gloss over. When the private instance reaches out to, say, a Linux package repository, the NAT Gateway rewrites the source so the request looks like it's coming from the NAT Gateway's own Elastic IP, sends it out, and when the response comes back, it knows exactly which private instance to route it to because it's tracking that specific outbound flow. If a server on the internet instead tries to initiate a brand-new connection to that private instance's address, there's no matching outbound flow for the NAT Gateway to match it against — it simply has nothing to route it to, so the connection goes nowhere. That's fundamentally different from a firewall rule that's just blocking inbound traffic; the NAT Gateway was never built to accept new inbound connections in the first place, which is exactly why it's the standard pattern for giving a private subnet patching and API access without ever making it reachable from outside.
commonMistakes: Describing a NAT Gateway as a firewall rather than explaining the actual flow-tracking mechanism
Forgetting the NAT Gateway itself must live in a public subnet, not the private subnet it serves
Not knowing the NAT Gateway needs an Elastic IP to function
Assuming a NAT Gateway provides any inbound access at all, even restricted — it provides none
keyPoints: NAT Gateway allows outbound-only internet access for private-subnet instances
Return traffic is matched to an outbound flow the instance already started
There is no mechanism for a new inbound connection to reach the private instance through it
The NAT Gateway itself must be deployed in a public subnet with an Elastic IP

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the outbound-only behavior of a NAT Gateway
Correctly explains why return traffic is allowed but new inbound traffic is not
Notes the NAT Gateway must live in a public subnet with an Elastic IP
Distinguishes NAT Gateway behavior from a firewall/security group concept

questions.title: On-Demand vs. Reserved Instances vs. Savings Plans vs. Spot
questions.prompt: A company runs a production database, an autoscaling web tier, and a nightly batch job on EC2. Explain the four main EC2 pricing models and which one you'd pick for each of those three workloads, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: On-Demand is pay-by-the-hour with no commitment — the most expensive rate, but the most flexible, right for anything unpredictable. Reserved Instances commit to a specific instance family in a specific region for 1 or 3 years in exchange for a significant discount, often 40-60%. Savings Plans are a more flexible alternative: instead of committing to an instance family, you commit to a dollar-per-hour spend, and the discount applies automatically across instance families and sizes. Spot Instances run on spare EC2 capacity at a steep discount, commonly 60-90% off, but AWS can reclaim them with a short notice period. For the production database — steady, predictable, must never unexpectedly stop — a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan fits, since the usage pattern justifies the commitment. For the autoscaling web tier, On-Demand covers the unpredictable variable part, often layered with a Savings Plan covering the steady baseline load. For the nightly batch job that can simply restart if interrupted, Spot Instances are the right fit — the steep discount is worth the small risk of a reclaim notice on a job that tolerates one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd match each workload to its risk tolerance rather than just listing the four models. The database is the easy case — it's always running, the load is predictable, so committing to a Reserved Instance or a Savings Plan is free money; there's no scenario where On-Demand makes sense for something that never turns off. The web tier is trickier because it's genuinely variable — I don't know day to day how many instances I need — so I'd keep the bursty part On-Demand, but if I look at six months of data and see there's always at least, say, five instances running no matter what, I'd put a Savings Plan under that steady baseline and let only the burst above it stay On-Demand. The batch job is the interesting one: it can tolerate an interruption, it can just pick back up, so Spot is almost free money there too — 60 to 90 percent off for a workload where the one real risk, a two-minute reclaim notice, doesn't actually hurt because the job just requeues. The pattern I always come back to is: commitment where the usage is certain, Spot where interruption is cheap, On-Demand everywhere else.
commonMistakes: Recommending Spot Instances for the production database, ignoring the reclaim risk
Not distinguishing Reserved Instances (specific instance family/region) from Savings Plans (flexible dollar commitment)
Forgetting that On-Demand is still useful layered on top of a Savings Plan for the unpredictable portion of variable workloads
Assuming a Savings Plan requires committing to a specific instance type the way an RI does
keyPoints: On-Demand: no commitment, most expensive, right for unpredictable workloads
Reserved Instances: 1-3 year commitment to a specific family/region for a discount
Savings Plans: flexible dollar-per-hour commitment, discount applies across families
Spot: steep discount on spare capacity, reclaimable with short notice — right for interruption-tolerant workloads

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes all four pricing models
Correctly matches the database to RI/Savings Plan
Correctly matches the web tier to a blended On-Demand/Savings Plan approach
Correctly matches the batch job to Spot and explains why interruption tolerance matters

questions.title: Zero trust: identity as the new perimeter
questions.prompt: Explain what 'zero trust' actually means in cloud networking, and why the phrase 'identity is the new perimeter' is the key shift from traditional network security.
questions.modelAnswer: Traditional network security assumed a hard perimeter: anything inside the corporate network (behind the firewall, on the VPN) was implicitly trusted, and security focused on keeping attackers outside that boundary. Zero trust rejects that assumption entirely — 'never trust, always verify' means no request is automatically trusted just because of where it came from on the network, including requests from inside what used to be the trusted perimeter. Instead, every request is verified based on identity, device health, and context, continuously, not just at initial login. 'Identity is the new perimeter' captures the practical consequence: since network location no longer implies trust, the thing actually being checked and gated on every request is who (or what) is asking and whether they're authorized for that specific action — not which network segment the request originated from. That's why conditional access policies, continuous verification, and microsegmentation all matter more in a zero trust model than a traditional firewall rule based on IP range.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this with the before-and-after, because that's what actually lands in an interview. The old model was castle-and-moat: get inside the VPN or the office network, and after that you were basically trusted to reach whatever you could see. The problem is that model falls apart the moment anyone or anything inside that network is compromised — a stolen laptop, a phished credential — because the attacker immediately inherits all of that implicit trust just by being on the inside. Zero trust throws out the idea that network location means anything at all. Every single request gets checked against identity and context, every time, regardless of where it's coming from. That's the real meaning behind 'identity is the new perimeter' — the perimeter used to be a network boundary you could draw on a diagram; now the thing actually enforcing the boundary is a continuous check on who's asking and whether their identity, device, and context justify this specific access, which is exactly what conditional access and microsegmentation are built to do.
commonMistakes: Describing zero trust as 'just more firewalls' rather than a shift away from network-based trust entirely
Thinking zero trust means verifying only once at login, rather than continuously
Not connecting the phrase 'identity is the new perimeter' to the practical shift toward conditional access policies
Assuming zero trust eliminates the need for network controls like microsegmentation, rather than complementing them
keyPoints: Traditional security trusted anything inside the network perimeter by default
Zero trust verifies every request by identity and context, regardless of network origin
Verification is continuous, not a one-time login check
Identity (not network location) becomes the thing actually being checked and gated

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the old castle-and-moat model it replaces
Correctly explains 'never trust, always verify'
Correctly explains why identity replaces network location as the perimeter
Mentions continuous verification, not just initial login

questions.title: Encryption at rest and the role of Key Vault / KMS
questions.prompt: Explain what 'encryption at rest' means in practice on Azure or AWS, and what role a service like Azure Key Vault or AWS KMS actually plays — what would be missing if you just said 'the disk is encrypted' without mentioning key management at all?
questions.modelAnswer: Encryption at rest means data stored on disk — a managed disk, a storage account blob, a database file — is encrypted so that someone with raw access to the underlying storage media can't read it without the encryption key. Both Azure and AWS encrypt data at rest by default on most services today. The part that's easy to skip is where the encryption key itself lives and who controls it — that's what Azure Key Vault and AWS KMS actually manage. Without a dedicated key management service, you either rely entirely on provider-managed keys (the provider generates, stores, and rotates the key, and you have no direct control over or visibility into it) or you'd have to build your own secure key storage and rotation, which is exactly the hard problem Key Vault/KMS exists to solve. The real value of Key Vault/KMS is customer-managed keys: the customer controls key creation, rotation, and revocation, and critically can revoke access to the key independently of the data itself — which matters for compliance requirements that specify who must be able to prove control over encryption keys, not just that encryption exists.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on 'the disk is encrypted' as an incomplete answer, because in an interview that phrase alone tells me someone hasn't thought about who holds the key. Encryption at rest, on its own, is table stakes now — Azure and AWS encrypt most things by default whether you ask for it or not. The actual decision point is whether you're using platform-managed keys, where the provider generates and rotates the key and you just trust it's handled, versus customer-managed keys through Key Vault or KMS, where you control the key's lifecycle yourself. The practical reason that distinction matters: if I need to prove, for a compliance audit, that I can revoke access to a dataset independently of deleting the dataset itself, platform-managed keys can't give me that — only a customer-managed key I control through Key Vault or KMS can, because I can disable or delete that key and instantly make the data unreadable without touching the data at all. That's the detail that separates 'encryption exists' from 'encryption that actually satisfies a real governance requirement.'
commonMistakes: Treating 'encryption at rest' as a complete answer without mentioning key ownership
Not distinguishing platform-managed keys from customer-managed keys
Assuming Key Vault/KMS is only for secrets like passwords, not for managing encryption keys themselves
Forgetting that revoking a customer-managed key can make data unreadable without deleting the data
keyPoints: Encryption at rest protects data on disk from anyone with raw storage access
Azure/AWS encrypt most data by default, but the key's ownership is the real variable
Platform-managed keys: provider controls the full key lifecycle
Customer-managed keys via Key Vault/KMS: customer controls creation, rotation, and revocation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what encryption at rest protects against
Correctly explains the role of Key Vault/KMS in key management
Distinguishes platform-managed from customer-managed keys
Gives a concrete reason customer-managed keys matter (e.g. independent revocation)

questions.title: Why Terraform needs a state file
questions.prompt: Explain what's actually inside terraform.tfstate, and why Terraform can't function correctly without it — what would go wrong if Terraform tried to operate with no memory of what it had already created?
questions.modelAnswer: terraform.tfstate is a JSON file that maps every resource block in your configuration to the real-world object Terraform believes exists in the cloud — its resource ID, every attribute Terraform knows about it, and enough metadata to diff 'what's declared' against 'what's really there' on the next plan. Without it, Terraform has no memory between runs. Every time you ran plan or apply, Terraform would have no way to know whether a resource block describing, say, an Azure resource group already corresponds to a real resource group or not — it would have to guess, and guessing wrong means either a failed apply (trying to create something that already exists) or, worse, silently creating a duplicate resource because Terraform thinks nothing exists yet. The state file is what lets plan answer the actually useful question — 'what, specifically, needs to change to make reality match my config' — instead of 'create everything from scratch every time.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the state file as Terraform's only memory, because that's the thing that actually explains every weird behavior people run into with it. Terraform's config files describe desired end state, but they don't track what already exists — that's the state file's entire job. Without it, every plan would be comparing your config against nothing, which means Terraform's only honest answer would be 'create all of this,' even against infrastructure that's already sitting there running in production. That's exactly why a teammate who checks out your Terraform config but doesn't have a copy of your state file gets a plan that wants to create everything from scratch — not because Terraform is broken, but because, from that teammate's machine's point of view, nothing exists yet. It's also exactly why the state file has to be shared, not local to one laptop — which is the whole reason remote backends exist.
commonMistakes: Saying Terraform 'reads the cloud directly' to know what exists — it relies on the state file as its primary source of truth for planning
Not explaining what specifically is recorded in the state (resource IDs, attributes, metadata)
Confusing the state file with the .tf configuration files — the config describes desired state, the state file records actual state
Missing that this is exactly why a teammate without a copy of the state file sees a plan to 'create everything'

It's Terraform's only memory of what already exists between runs
Without it, plan can't distinguish 'already exists' from 'needs to be created'
This is why state has to be shared across a team, not left on one person's laptop

questions.title: The real relationship between a Pod, a ReplicaSet, and a Deployment
questions.prompt: Explain why almost nobody writes a bare Kubernetes ReplicaSet directly, and what a Deployment adds on top of it that a ReplicaSet alone can't do.
questions.modelAnswer: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit, but on its own it has no self-healing or scaling — if the node it's on dies, it's gone for good. A ReplicaSet wraps a Pod template and a replica count and runs a reconciliation loop that only checks quantity: if the number of matching Pods drops below the desired count, it creates replacements. But a ReplicaSet never edits a running Pod and has no concept of changing its own template safely — if you update the image in a ReplicaSet's spec, existing Pods keep running the old image forever, because a ReplicaSet reconciles count, never content. A Deployment sits one layer above the ReplicaSet specifically to manage that gap: when you change a Deployment's Pod template, it creates a brand-new ReplicaSet with the new template, scales it up gradually while scaling the old ReplicaSet down, and deletes the old ReplicaSet once the new one is healthy — a controlled rolling update. That's the entire reason almost nobody writes a bare ReplicaSet: it can keep a fixed number of Pods running, but it can't roll out a change to them without a human manually deleting Pods one at a time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always answer this by pointing at exactly what each layer's reconciliation loop checks, because that's the detail that actually shows understanding instead of just naming the objects. A ReplicaSet's loop checks one thing: how many Pods matching my template currently exist, versus how many should? If a Pod disappears, it creates a replacement — that's it, that's the whole loop. It has zero mechanism for changing what's already running. So the moment you need to ship a new image version, a bare ReplicaSet leaves you manually deleting Pods and hoping the ReplicaSet controller replaces them with the new template fast enough that you don't take the app down mid-rollout — which is a genuinely bad way to deploy anything. A Deployment exists specifically to own that problem: changing a Deployment's template doesn't touch existing Pods at all, it creates an entirely new ReplicaSet with the new template, and then manages scaling the new one up and the old one down together, which is what a rolling update actually is under the hood. That's why I'd tell someone: you basically never write a ReplicaSet by hand — you write a Deployment, and Kubernetes creates and manages the ReplicaSet for you as an implementation detail.
commonMistakes: Saying a ReplicaSet can update Pods' content — it only ever creates or deletes whole Pods to match a count
Describing a Deployment as directly managing Pods, skipping the ReplicaSet layer it actually creates and owns
Not explaining that a template change creates a brand-new ReplicaSet rather than modifying the existing one
Confusing the label-selector mechanism (how a ReplicaSet finds 'its' Pods) with a naming or ownership pointer
keyPoints: A ReplicaSet's reconciliation loop only checks and fixes Pod count, never content
Editing a ReplicaSet's template does not change already-running Pods
A Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet per template change and manages scaling old/new together
This is what makes a controlled rolling update possible, which is why Deployments are used almost universally over bare ReplicaSets

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the Pod's limitation (no self-healing on its own)
Correctly describes the ReplicaSet's count-only reconciliation loop
Correctly describes what a Deployment adds (new ReplicaSet per template change, managed rollout)

questions.title: SLI, SLO, and error budget
questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between an SLI, an SLO, and an error budget, and why a 99.9% SLO measured over 30 days is a meaningfully different commitment than 99.9% measured over a single day.
questions.modelAnswer: An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a single, concrete, measured metric reflecting user-facing experience, usually expressed as a ratio — availability (successful requests / total requests), latency (percent of requests under some threshold), and so on. An SLO (Service Level Objective) attaches a target and a time window to that SLI: '99.9% of requests succeed, measured over a rolling 30 days.' An error budget is simply 100% minus the SLO target — the amount of unreliability the team is allowed to spend before it must slow down and prioritize reliability work over new features. The time window matters as much as the percentage: 99.9% over 30 days allows roughly 43 minutes of downtime across the whole month, so a short, sharp outage barely dents it. The same 99.9% measured over a single day allows only about 1.4 minutes that day — a single short outage could consume the entire daily budget at once, making a daily SLO a much stricter, more volatile commitment than the same percentage measured monthly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the actual math, because that's what separates someone who's memorized the vocabulary from someone who understands why the window matters. If my SLO is 99.9% over 30 days, my error budget is 0.1% of that 30-day window, which works out to about 43 minutes total I'm allowed to be down or failing requests across the entire month. If instead someone measured that same 99.9% target over a single day, the allowed budget shrinks to roughly 1.4 minutes for that one day — and one real incident, even a short one, can blow through the whole thing instantly. That's the practical difference: a monthly window smooths out a single bad day, while a daily window makes every single incident existentially threatening to that day's target. In an interview I'd also connect this to why the error budget matters beyond the math — it's what turns 'is this reliable enough to ship a risky change this week' from a gut-feel argument into a number: if the budget still has room, ship it; if it's nearly spent, that's the signal to freeze and go fix reliability instead of debating it.
commonMistakes: Defining SLO and SLA as the same thing — SLO is internal, SLA is the external contractual promise
Forgetting the time window is as important as the percentage target
Not being able to do the actual math (0.1% of 30 days ≈ 43 minutes) when asked
Treating the error budget as just a reporting number rather than a decision-making input for whether to ship
keyPoints: SLI: a measured, user-facing metric (availability, latency, etc.)
SLO: a target plus a time window attached to an SLI
Error budget = 100% minus the SLO target
A shorter measurement window makes the same percentage target a much stricter, more volatile commitment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines SLI
Correctly defines SLO including the time window
Correctly defines error budget and does the math for the 30-day example
Explains why the daily vs. monthly window produces a meaningfully different commitment

questions.title: Fixing a permission string with chmod
questions.prompt: A deploy script on a Linux server shows permissions rw-r--r-- on deploy.sh. Nobody but root can execute it. Write the single chmod command, in octal, that adds execute permission for the owner while leaving everyone else's permissions unchanged, and explain how you got that number.
questions.code:
$ ls -l deploy.sh
-rw-r--r--  1 jsmith developers  812 Oct 28 09:00 deploy.sh
questions.modelAnswer: The current permissions are rw-r--r--: owner has read+write (rw-), group has read-only (r--), everyone else has read-only (r--). Converting each triplet to octal: rw- = 4+2+0 = 6, r-- = 4+0+0 = 4, r-- = 4. So the current mode is 644. Adding execute for the owner only means changing the owner's triplet from rw- (6) to rwx (4+2+1 = 7), while leaving group and other untouched at 4 and 4. The command is chmod 744 deploy.sh. After that, ls -l shows -rwxr--r--: the owner can read, write, and execute; group and everyone else remain read-only, exactly as before.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always do the octal conversion triplet by triplet out loud so I don't make an arithmetic mistake under pressure. Owner's current bits are rw-, which is read (4) plus write (2), no execute (0), so that's 6. I want to add execute, which is worth 1, so 6 plus 1 is 7 — that's rwx. Group and other are both staying exactly as they are: r-- is 4, and I'm not touching them. So the full mode string is 7-4-4, and the command is chmod 744 deploy.sh. If I wanted to be extra explicit instead of reasoning in octal, I'd use the symbolic form chmod u+x deploy.sh, which says the same thing in English — add execute for the user/owner only — and is a good sanity check against the octal math if I'm ever unsure.
questions.example:
$ chmod 744 deploy.sh
$ ls -l deploy.sh
-rwxr--r--  1 jsmith developers  812 Oct 28 09:00 deploy.sh

# Equivalent symbolic form:
$ chmod u+x deploy.sh
commonMistakes: Using chmod 755, which also grants group and other execute permission that wasn't asked for
Miscounting the octal values (forgetting execute = 1, write = 2, read = 4)
Using chmod +x deploy.sh without the u flag, which can add execute for everyone depending on umask behavior
Confusing which triplet is owner vs. group vs. other when reading ls -l output
keyPoints: rw-r--r-- converts to octal 644
Adding execute only for the owner changes the first digit from 6 to 7
The correct command is chmod 744 deploy.sh
chmod u+x deploy.sh is the symbolic equivalent and a good sanity check

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly converts the current rwx string to octal
Correctly identifies only the owner's triplet needs to change
Produces the correct command, chmod 744
Correctly explains the resulting permission string

questions.title: Scoping an Azure Contributor role with the CLI
questions.prompt: Using the Azure CLI, assign the finance team's security group the Contributor role, scoped only to the resource group rg-finance-app — not the whole subscription. Write the command.
questions.modelAnswer: The az role assignment create command takes the assignee (the security principal's object ID), the role name, and a --scope flag that must point at the specific resource group's full resource ID, not the subscription. Getting the scope right is the entire point of the exercise: passing the subscription ID alone as scope would grant Contributor across every resource group in the subscription, not just the finance team's.
questions.professionalAnswer: The command itself is short, but the thing I'd narrate out loud in an interview is why the --scope value has to be the resource group's full resource ID path, not just its name or the subscription ID. If I got lazy and scoped this to the subscription because it was 'easier,' I'd be handing the finance group Contributor over every other team's resources too — which is exactly the least-privilege mistake this kind of task is designed to catch. I'd also mention that I'd grab the security group's object ID with az ad group show first rather than guessing it, since assigning a role to the wrong principal silently grants access to nothing the finance team actually needed.
questions.code: az ad group show --group "finance-team" --query id -o tsv
questions.example:
GROUP_ID=$(az ad group show --group "finance-team" --query id -o tsv)

az role assignment create \
  --assignee "$GROUP_ID" \
  --role "Contributor" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/rg-finance-app"
commonMistakes: Scoping the assignment to the subscription instead of the specific resource group
Assigning the role to a user instead of the security group, making it harder to manage membership over time
Forgetting the --scope value must be a full resource ID path, not just the resource group name
Using the Owner role instead of Contributor when the team only needs to manage resources, not grant access to others

--scope must be the full resource ID of the resource group to limit the grant correctly
Assigning to a group rather than an individual user is the better practice for ongoing management
Contributor, not Owner, is correct when the team doesn't need to grant access to others

Scopes correctly to the resource group's full resource ID, not the subscription
Assigns to the group's object ID rather than guessing or hardcoding
Uses Contributor rather than a broader role like Owner

questions.title: Tagging AWS resources for cost tracking
questions.prompt: Using the AWS CLI, tag an existing EC2 instance with team=payments and environment=prod so it shows up correctly in Cost Explorer once cost allocation tags are activated.
questions.modelAnswer: The aws ec2 create-tags command applies one or more key/value tags to a resource by its ID. Tagging the instance is only half the job, though — a tag has to also be activated as a Cost Allocation Tag in the Billing console before Cost Explorer will let anyone group or filter spend by it. It's also worth applying the tags consistently: team and environment should use a fixed, agreed-upon casing (team=payments, not Payments or Team) across every resource, because inconsistent casing fragments the same logical group into multiple buckets in cost reports.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd apply the tags with aws ec2 create-tags and then immediately flag the step most people forget: tagging the resource doesn't make it usable in Cost Explorer by itself. The tag has to be activated as a Cost Allocation Tag in Billing, a one-time step per tag key, before any report can group or filter by it. I'd also bring up the consistency problem unprompted, because it's the kind of thing that quietly breaks FinOps reporting for months before anyone notices — if one engineer tags something environment=prod and another tags theirs environment=Production, those are two different buckets to Cost Explorer even though they mean the same thing to a human. In a real environment I'd rather enforce this with an Azure Policy-equivalent AWS Organizations tag policy than trust everyone to type it correctly by hand every time.

aws ec2 create-tags \
  --resources i-0abc123456789def0 \
  --tags Key=team,Value=payments Key=environment,Value=prod

Using inconsistent casing or values across resources (prod vs. Production), fragmenting cost reports
Tagging the instance but forgetting associated resources like its EBS volumes, which incur their own cost separately
Not knowing AWS Organizations tag policies exist to enforce tag consistency at the platform level

A tag must be activated as a Cost Allocation Tag in Billing before Cost Explorer can use it
Tag value consistency (exact casing/spelling) matters as much as tag existence
Related resources (like EBS volumes) may need their own tags to be fully cost-attributed

questions.title: Writing an idempotent PowerShell provisioning check
questions.prompt: Write a PowerShell snippet that creates an Azure resource group named rg-prod in eastus, but is safe to run any number of times without erroring on the second run.
questions.modelAnswer: The idiomatic idempotent pattern is check-then-act: use Get-AzResourceGroup with -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue to check whether the resource group already exists without throwing an error if it doesn't, and only call New-AzResourceGroup if that check comes back empty. Calling New-AzResourceGroup unconditionally works the first time but throws an error on every subsequent run, because the resource group already exists by then — which is exactly the failure mode idempotency is meant to prevent.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as check-then-act every time, because it's the one pattern that generalizes to almost every automation script in this path, not just resource groups. Get-AzResourceGroup with -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue is the key piece — without that flag, checking for something that doesn't exist yet would itself throw an error and stop the script, which defeats the purpose. With it, the cmdlet just returns nothing if the resource group isn't there, I check that with an if, and only call New-AzResourceGroup when I actually need to create it. Run this script once, it creates rg-prod. Run it five more times — a pipeline retry, a teammate rerunning it, whatever — and it does nothing on each of those runs, silently confirming the resource group is already in the correct state, instead of throwing 'resource group already exists' and failing a pipeline that didn't actually need to fail.
commonMistakes: Calling New-AzResourceGroup directly with no existence check, which fails on the second run
Forgetting -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue on the check, which causes the check itself to throw when nothing is found
Wrapping the whole thing in try/catch instead of checking first — this works but obscures the actual intent and makes a real error harder to distinguish from 'already exists'
Not applying the same check-then-act pattern consistently to other resources created later in the same script
keyPoints: Idempotent means safe to run any number of times with the same end result
The pattern is check-then-act: verify existence before creating
-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue prevents the existence check itself from throwing
This pattern generalizes to any resource type, not just resource groups

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses a check-then-act pattern rather than an unconditional create
Correctly uses Get-AzResourceGroup with -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Script is syntactically valid PowerShell
Explains why this specifically makes the script safe to rerun

questions.title: Authenticating a Python script to AWS and Azure
questions.prompt: You need a Python script that can create resources in both AWS (via boto3) and Azure (via the Azure SDK) without hardcoding any credentials in the script itself. Describe how each SDK authenticates, and show how you'd structure the code.
questions.modelAnswer: boto3 authenticates using a credential chain: it checks environment variables, then the shared credentials file (~/.aws/credentials), then an IAM role if running on AWS infrastructure like EC2 or Lambda, picking up whichever is available without the script ever referencing a key directly. The Azure SDK for Python uses azure.identity's DefaultAzureCredential, which similarly tries a chain — environment variables, a managed identity if running on Azure infrastructure, then Azure CLI credentials if you're logged in locally — again with no secret hardcoded in the script. In both cases the script just instantiates a client/session and lets the SDK's default credential chain resolve the actual credential at runtime, which means the exact same code can run locally (using your CLI login or local env vars) and in a pipeline or on a VM (using a managed identity or instance role) without any code change.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I always emphasize here is that the script itself should never know or care where the credential actually comes from — that's the whole point of using the default credential chain instead of hardcoding anything. For boto3, I just create a boto3.client or Session with no explicit key arguments, and it resolves credentials itself: env vars first, then the shared credentials file, then an instance role if it's running on EC2. For Azure, DefaultAzureCredential does the same job: it'll pick up a managed identity if the script's running on an Azure VM or in a pipeline with workload identity federation configured, or fall back to my own az login session if I'm running it from my laptop. The payoff is that I can write and test this script locally against my own CLI login, then deploy the exact same code to a pipeline or a VM with a managed identity attached, and it authenticates correctly in both places with zero code changes — which is also exactly why hardcoding a key ever feels like a shortcut but never actually is one.
questions.code:
import boto3
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.mgmt.resource import ResourceManagementClient

# boto3: credential chain resolves automatically (env vars, ~/.aws/credentials, instance role)
ec2 = boto3.client("ec2", region_name="us-east-1")

# Azure: DefaultAzureCredential resolves automatically (env vars, managed identity, az cli login)
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
resource_client = ResourceManagementClient(credential, subscription_id="00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000")
commonMistakes: Passing access_key/secret_key arguments directly into boto3.client(), hardcoding credentials in the script
Not knowing DefaultAzureCredential tries multiple sources in a defined order rather than requiring one specific method
Assuming a script written for local development needs changes before it can run under a managed identity
Forgetting that a managed identity or instance role still needs to be granted the right permissions separately from 'just working'
keyPoints: boto3 resolves credentials via a chain: env vars, shared credentials file, then instance role
Azure SDK's DefaultAzureCredential resolves via a similar chain ending in managed identity or CLI login
Neither SDK requires hardcoding a key in the script itself
The same code can run locally and in production without modification, only the resolved credential source differs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes boto3's credential chain
Correctly describes DefaultAzureCredential's chain

questions.title: Parsing CLI JSON output with jq
questions.prompt: Write a one-line bash command that lists all AWS EC2 instance IDs and their current state, using the AWS CLI's JSON output piped through jq, without using any other text-processing tool.
questions.modelAnswer: aws ec2 describe-instances returns a deeply nested JSON structure, where instances are nested inside Reservations[].Instances[]. jq's .[] iterates arrays, and a jq filter can flatten both levels in one expression, projecting just the InstanceId and the nested State.Name field for each instance. Piping the CLI's --output json (the default) into jq avoids writing a separate script or using grep/awk against unstructured text, which is fragile against any change in field ordering or formatting.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for jq here instead of grep or awk specifically because the output is structured JSON, not line-oriented text — trying to regex-match an instance ID out of aws ec2 describe-instances with grep works until AWS reformats the output slightly, and then it silently breaks. The filter itself walks the actual shape of the JSON: Reservations is an array, so .Reservations[] iterates it; each reservation has an Instances array, so .Instances[] iterates that too; and then I pull InstanceId and the nested State.Name directly by path. I'd run it with -r to get raw unquoted output instead of JSON-quoted strings, since I usually want this piped into something else afterward, like a loop or a CSV.

Forgetting the double .[] needed to flatten Reservations and Instances, which are both arrays
Omitting -r, leaving the output wrapped in JSON string quotes instead of raw text
Not knowing State is itself a nested object (State.Name), not a flat field on the instance

-r produces raw text output instead of JSON-quoted strings
Using jq instead of grep/awk avoids fragility against JSON formatting changes

questions.title: Writing a reusable Terraform network module
questions.prompt: Write a minimal Terraform module that creates an Azure VNet, taking the VNet name and address space as input variables, and show how you'd call it for a dev environment.
questions.modelAnswer: A module is just a folder of .tf files with its own input variables (declared with variable blocks) and, usually, outputs. The module's main.tf declares the azurerm_virtual_network resource using the input variables instead of hardcoded values, so the same module folder produces a different VNet depending on what's passed in. Calling it from a root configuration uses a module block with a source pointing at the module's folder and values for each input variable — the same pattern repeated for staging or prod with different variable values, but calling the exact same reviewed HCL every time.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd make sure comes across is that a module isn't a special Terraform feature — it's just a folder with its own variables and resources, called the same way you'd call a function in any language. Inside modules/network, I'd declare vnet_name and address_space as input variables, then write the azurerm_virtual_network resource referencing those variables instead of literal strings. From the dev environment's root config, I call that module with module "network" { source = "../modules/network" ... } and pass in dev's specific name and CIDR range. If staging needs the identical structure with a different name and address space, I call the same module again with different inputs — I'm not copy-pasting the resource block a second time, I'm reusing the exact same reviewed configuration, which is the entire value of extracting it into a module in the first place.

questions.title: Configuring a Terraform remote backend
questions.prompt: Write the Terraform backend configuration to store state in an Azure Storage Account instead of locally, and explain what problem this specifically solves.
questions.modelAnswer: A backend block inside the terraform block configures where state is stored. For Azure, the azurerm backend type points at a specific storage account, container, and blob key where the state file will live remotely instead of on local disk. This solves the one-laptop problem directly: once state lives in a shared, remote location, every teammate running plan or apply reads and writes the same state, instead of each person's local checkout having no state at all and wanting to 'create everything.' It also enables locking — the azurerm backend supports native state locking via blob leases, preventing two people from running apply at the same moment and corrupting or overwriting each other's changes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame the backend block as solving exactly two problems, because that's what actually gets asked as a follow-up: shared source of truth, and locking. Before this, state sits in whatever folder I ran terraform apply from, which means it's local to my machine only — a teammate who clones the repo and runs plan has no state file at all, so Terraform assumes nothing exists yet and wants to recreate everything. Pointing the backend at an azurerm storage account container fixes that: now everyone's plan and apply reads and writes the exact same remote state file, so there's one shared truth instead of as many 'truths' as there are laptops. The second thing the azurerm backend buys automatically is locking via blob leases — if I'm mid-apply, the state blob is leased, and a teammate who tries to apply at the same moment gets blocked instead of racing me and corrupting the file. I'd run terraform init right after adding this block, since that's the step that actually migrates existing local state into the new backend.

Using the same key (blob name) for multiple environments, causing them to overwrite each other's state
Not realizing the azurerm backend provides locking automatically via blob leases, and assuming locking requires extra setup
Storing the storage account's access key directly in the backend block instead of using Azure AD authentication or environment variables

The azurerm backend stores state in a specific storage account/container/blob key
This solves the shared-source-of-truth problem for a team
The azurerm backend also provides state locking via blob leases

questions.title: A multi-stage Dockerfile that stays small
questions.prompt: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a Go application that keeps the final image small by not shipping build tools in the runtime image.
questions.modelAnswer: A multi-stage build uses two or more FROM statements in the same Dockerfile: an early build stage with the full compiler/SDK needed to build the application, and a final runtime stage that starts from a minimal base image and copies only the compiled binary out of the build stage using COPY --from=. Everything the build stage installed — the Go toolchain, build caches, intermediate files — never makes it into the final image, because the final stage never inherits from the build stage's filesystem, only whatever is explicitly copied out of it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key move in a multi-stage Dockerfile is naming the build stage with AS builder and then referencing it by that name in the final stage's COPY --from=builder line — everything else follows from that. In the build stage, I'd use the full golang image, which has the compiler and everything needed to produce a binary, and run go build to produce it. The final stage starts completely fresh from something minimal like alpine or even scratch, and the only thing it takes from the build stage is the compiled binary itself — nothing else from that first stage exists in the final image at all. That's the whole trick: the final image never sees the Go compiler, the module cache, or any of the intermediate build artifacts, so it ends up a tiny fraction of the size of a naive single-stage build that just installed Go and ran the app from the same image.
questions.code:
# Stage 1: build
FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app ./cmd/server

# Stage 2: runtime
FROM alpine:3.19
COPY --from=builder /app /app
USER nobody
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
commonMistakes: Using a single FROM and installing both build tools and the app in the same final image
Forgetting to name the build stage (AS builder) and then having nothing to reference in --from=
Not setting CGO_ENABLED=0 when targeting a minimal base like alpine or scratch, causing a runtime linking failure
Copying unnecessary files (like the full source tree) into the final stage instead of just the compiled binary
keyPoints: Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM statements, with earlier stages named for reference
COPY --from=<stage> pulls only specific artifacts out of an earlier stage
The final image never inherits the build stage's filesystem automatically
This keeps build tools and intermediate files entirely out of the shipped image

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly structures two distinct stages with FROM ... AS builder
Correctly uses COPY --from=builder to pull only the compiled artifact
Final stage uses a minimal base image
Explains why this keeps the final image small

questions.title: Hardening a Dockerfile to run as a non-root user
questions.prompt: Modify a Dockerfile so the application runs as a dedicated non-root user instead of the default root, including setting correct file ownership.
questions.modelAnswer: Unless a Dockerfile specifies otherwise, the process inside the container starts as root. Hardening it means creating a dedicated unprivileged user and group with groupadd/useradd, giving that user ownership of the application's files (using --chown on the COPY instruction, which sets ownership at copy time rather than needing a separate RUN chown layer), and adding a USER instruction before the final CMD/ENTRYPOINT — everything from that line onward, including the app's own process, runs as that unprivileged user instead of root.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd make the USER line the thing I explain most carefully, because it's the one instruction that actually changes runtime behavior — everything before it in the Dockerfile can still run as root during the build (installing packages, for instance), but once USER app appears, every instruction after it, including the CMD that actually starts the application, runs as that unprivileged user. I'd use --chown=app:app directly on the COPY instruction rather than a separate RUN chown step afterward, because that avoids creating an extra filesystem layer just to fix ownership. If I wanted to go further, I'd mention that distroless images like gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot already run as a fixed non-root UID out of the box, so sometimes the better hardening move is switching base images entirely rather than adding these lines by hand.
questions.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app -d /app -s /sbin/nologin app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=app:app . .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
USER app
CMD ["python", "main.py"]
commonMistakes: Adding the USER instruction but never fixing file ownership, leaving the app unable to read/write its own files
Running RUN chown as a separate step after COPY instead of using --chown directly, wasting an image layer
Placing USER before steps that genuinely need root (like package installation), breaking the build
Assuming running as non-root alone is sufficient hardening without considering read-only filesystems or capability drops
keyPoints: Containers run as root (UID 0) by default unless a Dockerfile says otherwise
USER switches the process UID for every instruction after it, including the final CMD
--chown=user:group on COPY sets ownership at copy time, avoiding an extra layer
Distroless non-root base images can achieve the same result with less Dockerfile code

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Creates a dedicated unprivileged user and group
Correctly sets file ownership using --chown
Places USER before CMD/ENTRYPOINT but after any steps requiring root
Explains what USER actually changes at runtime

lessonLink.label: Review: Running as a Non-Root User

questions.title: Writing a Kubernetes Service manifest
questions.prompt: Write a Kubernetes Service manifest that exposes a Deployment labeled app: payments-api internally within the cluster only, on port 80, forwarding to the container's port 8080.
questions.modelAnswer: A Service identifies its target Pods through a label selector matching the Deployment's Pod labels, not by name. Since the requirement is internal-only access, the type should be ClusterIP — which is also the default if type is omitted entirely. The port field is what clients send traffic to on the Service's own virtual IP, and targetPort is the actual port the container is listening on inside the Pod; those two don't have to match, and here they explicitly don't (80 vs. 8080).
questions.professionalAnswer: The two things I'd get right here are the selector and the port mapping, because those are the two ways people most often get a working-looking Service that silently routes nowhere. The selector has to match the exact labels the Deployment is stamping onto its Pods — app: payments-api — not the Deployment's own name, since Services never reference Pods by name at all. Then for the ports: clients talking to this Service hit port 80 on its virtual IP, and the Service forwards that to targetPort 8080, which is whatever port the container inside the Pod is actually listening on. Since the requirement says internal-only, I'd either explicitly set type: ClusterIP or just leave type out entirely, since that's the default — I wouldn't reach for NodePort or LoadBalancer here, since both of those expose the Service beyond the cluster, which isn't what was asked for.
questions.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: payments-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
commonMistakes: Setting type to NodePort or LoadBalancer when only internal access was requested
Using the Deployment's name as the selector instead of matching the Pod's actual labels
Confusing port (what clients hit) with targetPort (what the container actually listens on)
Forgetting the selector must match exactly, since Services find Pods by label, never by name
keyPoints: A Service finds Pods via a label selector, never by name
ClusterIP is the default type and is correct for internal-only access
port is the Service's own exposed port; targetPort is the container's actual listening port
The selector must exactly match the labels the Deployment applies to its Pods

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sets type to ClusterIP (or omits it)
Correctly sets the selector to match app: payments-api
Correctly maps port 80 to targetPort 8080
YAML is syntactically valid

questions.title: Writing a KQL query to find failed requests
questions.prompt: Write a Log Analytics KQL query that returns the count of failed HTTP requests (status code 500 or higher) per hour, over the last 24 hours, from a table called AppRequests with columns TimeGenerated and ResponseCode.
questions.modelAnswer: The query starts from the AppRequests table, filters to the last 24 hours and failed requests (ResponseCode >= 500), then uses summarize with bin() to group results into one-hour buckets based on TimeGenerated. bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) is the specific function that rounds each row's timestamp down to its containing hour, which is what makes the count group by hour rather than returning one row per individual request.
questions.professionalAnswer: The piece of this that actually matters is bin(), because that's the function doing the hourly bucketing — without it, summarize count() by TimeGenerated would just group by the exact timestamp, which is effectively one bucket per request since timestamps are nearly all unique. bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) rounds every timestamp down to its containing hour, so all the failed requests between, say, 14:00:00 and 14:59:59 collapse into one row. I'd filter first — where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) and ResponseCode >= 500 — before the summarize, both because that's clearer to read and because KQL evaluates the pipeline top to bottom, so filtering early reduces how much data the summarize step has to process.
questions.code:
AppRequests
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResponseCode >= 500
| summarize FailedCount = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| order by TimeGenerated asc
commonMistakes: Summarizing by TimeGenerated directly instead of bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), producing one row per request instead of per hour
Filtering on ResponseCode == 500 instead of >= 500, missing 502, 503, 504, and other 5xx codes
Placing the time filter after the summarize instead of before it, processing unnecessary data
Forgetting order by, leaving the hourly buckets in an unpredictable order
keyPoints: where clauses filter rows; place time and status filters before summarize
bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) buckets timestamps into one-hour groups
ResponseCode >= 500 correctly captures all 5xx server error codes
summarize count() by <bucket> produces the per-hour count

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly filters to the last 24 hours using ago(24h)
Correctly filters failed requests with ResponseCode >= 500
Correctly uses bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) for hourly grouping
Query is syntactically valid KQL
